# Marin Lazic

> Performance coach for founders, training and recovery. Strength and Conditioning Coach for the Australian Men's Water Polo Team (the Aussie Sharks) and founder of Otion. Sydney, coaching online.

Last updated: 2026-10-16

## Who Marin Lazic is

Marin Lazic is the National Lead Strength and Conditioning Coach for the Australian Men's Water Polo Team, a role he has held since October 2021. He prepared the team for the Paris 2024 Olympic Games and for the 2023, 2024 and 2025 World Championships in Fukuoka, Doha and Singapore. He now supports the LA28 pathway. He first worked with the Australian national water polo program in 2015 during preparation for the Rio Olympics.

He has 15 years of experience in strength and conditioning. He holds ASCA Level 2 accreditation (Australian Strength and Conditioning Association) and a Certificate IV in Fitness. He was a TRX Master Instructor from 2008 to 2023 and a Trigger Point Master Trainer from 2012 to 2021.

As an athlete he played for the New Zealand Men's National Water Polo Team and in the Australian Water Polo League for Balmain Tigers, Drummoyne Devils and West Magpies. He trained under Hungarian coach Dénes Kemény.

He founded Otion in September 2023. Otion delivers health and performance coaching to founders, executives and organisations. He is based on Sydney's Northern Beaches, Australia.

## Services and pricing

- 1:1 executive performance coaching: $2,400 AUD per month, minimum 3 months. Delivered online. Programs run in Bridge Athletic. Apply at https://marinlazic.com/apply. No sales call. Marin reviews every application and replies by email.
- Free online Performance Assessment: 27 questions, about 5 minutes, produces a coaching score across sleep, stress, training, recovery, nutrition and injuries plus an AI assisted report. Not a clinical diagnosis. https://marinlazic.com/assessment
- Athlete performance programming for water polo and other sports.
- Corporate health and performance programs through Otion: https://marinlazic.com/corporate-health-performance
- Travel and jet lag protocols for athletes and professionals crossing time zones.

Coaching is education and training support. It is not medical diagnosis or treatment.

## Article reference content

### Creatine for Executives: A Practical, Evidence-Based Guide

Source: https://marinlazic.com/insights/creatine-complete-guide-for-executives
Published: 2026-03-14. Revised: 2026-10-14.

Creatine monohydrate at 3 to 5 grams a day is the best studied supplement in sport. It supports strength training, and the evidence on thinking and memory is early but promising.

Creatine is a compound stored mainly in muscle, with smaller stores in the brain. Phosphocreatine helps regenerate adenosine triphosphate (ATP) during short, demanding efforts. Food provides creatine, especially meat and fish, and the body also makes it. Supplementation can raise muscle creatine stores and support repeated high-intensity exercise. It is useful, but it is not a substitute for sleep, food, training or medical care.

## What does the evidence say creatine does?

Creatine monohydrate is the most studied form. Research supports benefits for repeated high-intensity exercise, strength and training adaptations when it is paired with suitable training. The [International Society of Sports Nutrition position stand](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC5469049/) describes creatine monohydrate as well studied and reports that muscle stores can be maintained with a daily dose after saturation.

Cognitive findings are promising but less settled than the exercise evidence. Some studies report benefits in memory or demanding tasks, with effects that may depend on diet, age, sleep loss and the task being tested. A review of common creatine questions notes that the evidence is mixed across outcomes and groups, so creatine should not be presented as a guaranteed focus aid or a treatment for fatigue. Better sleep remains the first response to regular sleep restriction.

## Which creatine should you buy?

Choose plain creatine monohydrate from a reputable seller. A brand does not need to be German-made to be suitable, and country of origin alone does not prove purity or risk. Avoid claims that one country is automatically safe and another is automatically contaminated.

Quality control matters because supplement manufacturing and labelling standards vary. In a survey of 33 products sold in Italy and produced in several countries, [Moret and colleagues](https://doi.org/10.1016/j.foodchem.2010.12.028) found creatinine above 100 mg/kg in 44% of samples. About 15% had detectable dihydro-1,3,5-triazine, with a maximum of 8.0 mg/kg, and some had dicyandiamide above 50 mg/kg. This study does not justify claims about all products from a particular country, and it does not establish that a specific brand is unsafe today.

Look for:

- A short ingredient list containing creatine monohydrate.
- A lot or batch number and a clear manufacturer or importer.
- Accessible testing or quality documentation where available.
- For tested athletes, a recognised programme such as [Informed Sport](https://sport.wetestyoutrust.com/), which says it tests every certified sports-supplement batch for banned substances before release. This reduces one category of risk. It is not a guarantee of performance or medical safety.

Third-party testing is a useful quality signal, not proof that one trade-marked source is the only suitable choice.

## How much creatine should you take and when?

For most adults, **3 to 5 grams of creatine monohydrate daily** is a common maintenance range. The appropriate amount can vary with body size, diet, training and individual circumstances. A universal formula such as 0.1 grams per kilogram is not mandatory.

A loading phase is optional. A common research protocol uses about 20 grams daily, split into smaller doses, for 5 to 7 days. This may raise muscle stores faster but can cause stomach upset for some people. Taking 3 to 5 grams daily reaches saturation more gradually, often over about 3 to 4 weeks. Timing is not important. Take it at a time you can repeat. Mixing it with a meal is reasonable, but there is no need for a special drink.

Drink to thirst and maintain normal hydration. Creatine can increase water held in muscle, and some people notice a change in body weight. That change is not automatically fat gain. Reduce the dose or stop and seek advice if persistent gastrointestinal symptoms occur.

## Is creatine safe, and who should check with a doctor first?

Evidence in healthy adults generally finds no harmful change in kidney function at recommended doses, but that does not make creatine suitable for everyone. Speak with a GP or pharmacist before using it if you have kidney disease, abnormal kidney tests, are pregnant or breastfeeding, are under 18, have a relevant medical condition, or take medicines that may affect kidney function or fluid balance. A clinician may want baseline or follow-up tests. Tell them that you use creatine, because creatine can affect blood creatinine readings without necessarily indicating a loss of kidney function.

Do not use this article to diagnose symptoms or replace prescribed treatment. Seek clinical care for ongoing exhaustion, mood changes, sleep problems, breathlessness, chest symptoms, marked swelling or other new symptoms.

## Does creatine help thinking and recovery?

Creatine may help some people with demanding cognitive work, but the size and reliability of any benefit remain uncertain. It cannot compensate for chronic sleep loss. Use it as one small part of a routine that includes regular meals, resistance training, aerobic work and a consistent sleep schedule.

## How should an executive start creatine?

1. Choose plain creatine monohydrate with clear batch information.
2. Start with 3 grams daily for a week, then consider 5 grams if it suits you and is appropriate for your circumstances.
3. Keep the timing simple and record tolerance, training and body-weight changes.
4. Review the plan with a clinician when health conditions or medicines are relevant.

For related recovery and training context, see [how to boost your HRV](/insights/how-to-boost-your-hrv) and the [Performance Assessment](/assessment). You can also explore the wider [insights](/insights) library.

## Sources

- [International Society of Sports Nutrition position stand: Safety and efficacy of creatine supplementation](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC5469049/)
- [Common questions and misconceptions about creatine supplementation](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC7871530/)
- [Moret et al., Levels of creatine, organic contaminants and heavy metals in creatine dietary supplements](https://doi.org/10.1016/j.foodchem.2010.12.028)

### How to Improve Sleep Quality: Practical Steps That Help

Source: https://marinlazic.com/insights/how-to-improve-sleep-quality
Published: 2026-03-10. Revised: 2026-10-14.

A fixed wake time, seven days a week, does more for sleep quality than any supplement or gadget. Everything else in this guide builds on that one habit.

## What does good sleep quality mean?

Good sleep is usually uninterrupted enough to feel restorative. Sleep duration and continuity both matter. Adults aged 18 to 60 are generally advised to get at least seven hours a night on a regular basis, although individual needs vary. [American Academy of Sleep Medicine and Sleep Research Society guidance](https://aasm.org/aasm-and-srs-publish-new-sleep-duration-consensus-statement/)

Wearable estimates of deep sleep, REM sleep and sleep stages can be useful for spotting broad patterns. They are not a diagnosis. Avoid treating one night or one score as proof that your body is recovering well or poorly.

## How do you improve sleep quality?

### 1. Make the bedroom quiet, dark and comfortable

Keep the room cool enough for comfort, reduce noise where possible, and use curtains or an eye mask if light enters the room. Put phones and work materials out of reach if they keep your mind active. A fan, earplugs or steady background sound may help. Adjust bedding or ventilation if you sleep hot.

### 2. Keep a stable wake time

Choose a wake time you can maintain most days. A regular schedule gives your body a useful cue, but bedtime should still follow your sleepiness. Sleep medicine treatments often prioritise a consistent wake time rather than forcing everyone into the same bedtime. Research on sleep hygiene also suggests that regularity can help, while the size of the benefit varies between people. [Sleep hygiene review](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC4400203/)

If weekends differ greatly from weekdays, shift gradually. Do not try to compensate for a short night by spending excessive time awake in bed.

### 3. Use light to support your body clock

Get outdoor light during the day, especially in the morning when practical. Keep evening lighting lower and warmer if bright light makes you feel alert. Turn off electronic devices at least 30 minutes before bed if they interfere with winding down. [Centers for Disease Control and Prevention sleep guidance](https://www.cdc.gov/sleep/about/index.html)

A strict screen ban is not required. Content, brightness, timing and sensitivity matter. If you need to work late, take short breaks and keep the screen as dim as is comfortable.

### 4. Check caffeine, alcohol and exercise

Caffeine can remain active for several hours, and sensitivity varies. If sleep is difficult, test moving coffee, energy drinks and pre-workout products earlier in the day. Alcohol may make you drowsy at first while disturbing sleep later. Large meals close to bed can also be uncomfortable.

Regular exercise may help sleep. Finish hard training early enough that it does not leave you overheated or alert at bedtime. A short walk, gentle stretching or easy breathing can suit the final part of the evening.

### 5. Build a low-stimulation wind-down

Use the final 30 to 60 minutes for a repeatable routine. Reading, a shower, light stretching, music or writing down tomorrow's tasks can help create a boundary around the day. If you are awake and frustrated, get out of bed for a quiet activity in low light. Return when sleepy rather than turning the bed into a place for worry.

Slow breathing can be a reasonable relaxation exercise. In a randomised study, five minutes a day of several breathing practices improved mood and reduced anxiety or respiratory rate. The study found no significant change in HRV, resting heart rate or sleep measures over 28 days. It therefore does not support a guaranteed sleep improvement or a fixed HRV percentage. [Breathing trial in *Cell Reports Medicine*](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC9873947/)

## How should you track sleep without chasing scores?

For two weeks, record bedtime, estimated time asleep, wake time, night waking, naps, caffeine, alcohol, exercise and how you felt during the day. Compare weekly patterns rather than reacting to one night. A wearable can add context, but its sleep-stage estimates are less reliable than a clinical sleep study. Focus on function: alertness, mood, concentration and whether sleep feels refreshing.

A template or session example in this article is **illustrative, not a real client result**. Your response may be different.

## When should you see a doctor about sleep?

Speak with a GP or qualified health professional if sleep problems persist, affect daily life, or occur with loud snoring, gasping, witnessed pauses in breathing, morning headaches, restless legs or severe daytime sleepiness. These signs can occur with sleep disorders that need assessment. Do not use sleep hygiene alone to manage suspected sleep apnoea, persistent insomnia, unusual movements or medication-related sleep problems. The [CDC advises speaking with a healthcare provider for regular sleep problems](https://www.cdc.gov/sleep/about/index.html).

Breathing exercises should be comfortable. Stop if you feel faint, distressed or short of breath. Seek urgent care for severe or sudden breathing difficulty, chest pain or other emergency symptoms.

## What should you do first?

Start with one or two changes: a stable wake time, less evening light, earlier caffeine, or a calmer bedroom. Keep them long enough to notice a pattern. There is no guaranteed result or perfect sleep score. If you want a broader review of recovery, training and lifestyle, [take the Performance Assessment](/assessment) or [apply to work together](/apply).

## Sources

- [Centers for Disease Control and Prevention: About Sleep](https://www.cdc.gov/sleep/about/index.html)
- [American Academy of Sleep Medicine and Sleep Research Society: adult sleep duration consensus](https://aasm.org/aasm-and-srs-publish-new-sleep-duration-consensus-statement/)
- [Irish et al., The Role of Sleep Hygiene in Promoting Public Health](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC4400203/)
- [Balban et al., Brief structured respiration practices enhance mood and reduce physiological arousal](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC9873947/)

### How to Boost Your HRV: A Practical, Evidence-Aware Guide

Source: https://marinlazic.com/insights/how-to-boost-your-hrv
Published: 2026-03-07. Revised: 2026-10-14.

Measure HRV at the same time each morning with the same device, and act on the weekly trend, not the daily score. Sleep timing, alcohol and training load move HRV more than any breathing drill does.

## Key points

Heart rate variability (HRV) is the variation in time between consecutive heartbeats. It reflects several interacting systems, including the autonomic nervous system, breathing, sleep, illness, training and stress. HRV is not a simple score for health, readiness or leadership performance. Higher is not always better, and one low reading is not a diagnosis. A [review of HRV metrics and norms](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC5624990/) stresses that recording length, age, sex and measurement context affect results.

The useful question is usually, “What is changing for me under similar conditions?” Use the same device and method, look at a run of readings, and note factors such as illness, alcohol, travel, hard training and poor sleep. Wearable methods and sampling schedules vary between brands, so do not compare numbers from different devices as if they were interchangeable. A [review of wearable HRV measurement](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC10742885/) also recommends focusing on individual trends rather than isolated snapshots.

## How do you raise HRV safely?

### 1. Protect regular sleep

Give sleep a consistent opportunity and keep your wake time reasonably stable. A practical starting point is the [sleep quality guide](/insights/how-to-improve-sleep-quality). Do not assume that a wearable’s sleep stages are exact, or that a target number of hours will suit every person. Loud snoring, witnessed pauses in breathing, gasping, persistent insomnia or marked daytime sleepiness warrant a GP or sleep clinician assessment.

### 2. Try calm, comfortable breathing

A few minutes of slow breathing can change HRV during the session. You could try a gentle inhale for four seconds and exhale for six, without straining or holding your breath. Stop if you feel dizzy, breathless or distressed.

Longer-term effects are less certain than the immediate change. In a randomised month-long study, five minutes of daily breathing improved mood and reduced respiratory rate, but it did **not** significantly change HRV, resting heart rate or sleep. See the [published trial](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC9873947/) for the full results. Treat breathing as a low-risk practice that may help calm you, not as a guaranteed way to raise your baseline HRV.

### 3. Build a steady aerobic base

Regular walking, cycling, swimming or rowing can support cardiovascular fitness. Use a pace at which you can speak in full sentences, then increase duration gradually. Public health activity guidance and your current fitness, injuries and medical history should shape the plan. There is no universal “Zone 2” heart-rate number that fits everyone.

### 4. Manage total load, not one score

Training, work pressure, travel, illness and reduced sleep can all affect recovery. If your HRV trend is lower than usual and you also feel unwell or unusually fatigued, choose an easier session, a walk or rest. Do not follow a rigid percentage rule. Consider your symptoms, performance, resting heart rate and recent workload together.

Burnout is not simply a low-HRV state. The [World Health Organization defines burn-out](https://www.who.int/news/item/28-05-2019-burn-out-an-occupational-phenomenon-international-classification-of-diseases) as an occupational phenomenon linked to chronic workplace stress, with exhaustion, mental distance or cynicism about work, and reduced professional efficacy. Persistent low mood, anxiety, severe exhaustion, substance reliance or thoughts of self-harm need qualified healthcare support rather than a wearable protocol.

### 5. Be realistic about alcohol and stimulants

Alcohol can disrupt sleep and may affect overnight HRV, but the size and duration of the effect vary with dose, timing and the person. Instead of promising a fixed percentage change, compare your own readings after alcohol-free periods and record what else changed. Keep caffeine earlier if it affects your sleep. If cutting down alcohol is difficult, speak with a GP or alcohol and other drug service.

## How should you track HRV week to week?

**Illustrative template, not a real client result:** For four weeks, measure HRV under the same conditions recommended by your device, preferably at a consistent time. Record sleep opportunity, alcohol, illness, training load and how you feel. Review weekly patterns rather than reacting to one number. Keep the device and measurement method the same throughout.

## When should you see a doctor about low HRV?

If HRV stays unusually low for you, or changes alongside palpitations, fainting, chest pain, severe breathlessness or illness, arrange a medical review. HRV cannot diagnose a heart, sleep, mental health or endocrine condition.

For a structured review of training, sleep and recovery, use the [Performance Assessment](/assessment) or [apply here](/apply). Use the information as coaching education, not a substitute for diagnosis or treatment.

## Sources

- [An Overview of Heart Rate Variability Metrics and Norms](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC5624990/)
- [Heart Rate Variability Measurement through a Smart Wearable Device](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC10742885/)
- [The effects of breathwork on stress, mood and physiological measures](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC9873947/)
- [WHO: Burn-out as an occupational phenomenon](https://www.who.int/news/item/28-05-2019-burn-out-an-occupational-phenomenon-international-classification-of-diseases)

### How to Lose Fat Without Losing Performance

Source: https://marinlazic.com/insights/how-to-lose-fat-without-losing-performance
Published: 2026-03-03. Revised: 2026-10-14.

You can lose fat and keep your strength if you keep lifting, eat enough protein and cut calories slowly. Crash dieting costs you the muscle you spent years building.

## Key takeaways

Fat loss requires an energy deficit over time. The eating pattern can vary, but no food, supplement or training method removes that requirement. A sensible plan uses a modest deficit, adequate protein, resistance training, regular movement and enough recovery. Results vary, and performance may fluctuate during a cut.

## How big should the calorie deficit be?

Estimate your usual intake and body-weight trend before changing anything. Tracking food, drinks, activity and sleep for several days can reveal where small changes are realistic. Apps such as [Cronometer](https://cronometer.com/) can help, although their calorie estimates are still estimates.

Choose a small change that you can maintain. This may mean smaller portions, fewer liquid calories, more filling foods, or a little more walking. A gradual rate is generally easier to maintain than rapid loss. The [CDC guidance on weight loss](https://www.cdc.gov/healthy-weight-growth/losing-weight/index.html) also notes that medicines, health conditions, stress, hormones and age can affect weight management.

Use a weekly average of body weight, plus waist measurements and gym performance. Daily weight changes often reflect fluid, food and glycogen. If your trend is not changing after a few weeks, review intake and activity rather than making a large cut straight away.

## How much protein and carbohydrate do you need while losing fat?

Protein helps support muscle protein synthesis and can make a calorie-controlled diet easier to manage. For many people who train, **1.4 to 2.0 grams of protein per kilogram of body weight per day** is a reasonable evidence-informed range. Higher intakes may be useful in some hypocaloric, resistance-trained settings, but they are not mandatory for everyone. These figures come from the [International Society of Sports Nutrition position stand on protein and exercise](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/28642676/).

Spread protein across meals that suit your routine. Meat, fish, eggs, yoghurt, tofu, beans and milk are useful options. Keep carbohydrate around demanding training when it helps you train well. Include vegetables, fruit, wholegrains and fats you enjoy.

## Should you keep lifting while losing fat?

Resistance training gives your body a reason to retain muscle while weight is coming down. Keep familiar lifts where possible, and use a range of movements that cover the major muscle groups. Squats, hinges, presses, rows and [chin-ups](/insights/how-to-do-a-chin-up) are examples, not a compulsory list.

Train two to four times per week if that fits your schedule. Keep effort reasonably high, but adjust sets, repetitions or exercise choices if recovery falls. Do not force planned numbers when technique is deteriorating, pain is increasing, or sleep and energy are poor. The right training load depends on your history, schedule and current health.

Cardio can support health and energy expenditure. Walking, cycling, swimming and other moderate activities are useful options. Start with an amount you can repeat, then add time or frequency gradually if recovery remains good. There is no universal step target or required “zone” for fat loss.

## Why do sleep and stress matter for fat loss?

Aim for a regular sleep routine and enough time in bed for you to function well. The [CDC weight-management guidance](https://www.cdc.gov/healthy-weight-growth/losing-weight/index.html) includes sleep and stress management as part of a healthy approach. Poor sleep can affect appetite, mood and training, but individual responses differ. Avoid claims that one breathing routine or sleep change will produce a fixed percentage improvement.

Short walks, planned breaks, daylight, enjoyable movement and slow breathing may help some people manage stress. Wearable HRV readings can be useful for observing **your own** device-specific trend over time. They are not a diagnosis and cannot provide certain readiness, recovery or health conclusions. A cold plunge has no guaranteed fat-loss, recovery or performance outcome.

## Should you take creatine while losing fat?

Creatine monohydrate can improve high-intensity training capacity for some people. A common adult maintenance approach is **3 to 5 grams per day**, if it is suitable for you. A loading phase is optional, not compulsory. Choose a product with clear ingredient information and, where possible, independent batch testing. Supplement quality can vary.

Creatine may increase scale weight through water stored in muscle. That is different from fat gain. Evidence for cognitive benefits is still developing, and effects may depend on the person and situation. Creatine is not a guarantee of better focus or performance. People with kidney disease, pregnancy, relevant medical conditions, or medicines that affect kidney function should speak with a clinician before using it. The [ISSN creatine position stand](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC5469049/) reviews safety evidence in healthy populations and the need for clinical context.

## What does a fat loss training day look like?

The following is an **illustrative template, not a real client result**: include protein-rich foods and produce across the day, keep carbohydrate around hard training, and use controlled sets of a squat, press, row, hinge and chin-up variation.

## When should you get professional help with fat loss?

Speak with a GP or accredited practising dietitian before major changes if you have diabetes, kidney or liver disease, a history of an eating disorder, are pregnant or breastfeeding, take regular medicines, or are losing weight without intending to. Seek help for persistent pain, severe fatigue or a continuing decline in performance and mood.

Track a few useful measures, make one change at a time, and allow enough time to judge the trend. For support with your starting point, use the [Performance Assessment](/assessment). You can also read the [sleep quality guide](/insights/how-to-improve-sleep-quality) and the [creatine guide](/insights/creatine-complete-guide-for-executives).

## Sources

- [CDC, Steps for Losing Weight](https://www.cdc.gov/healthy-weight-growth/losing-weight/index.html)
- [International Society of Sports Nutrition, Protein and Exercise position stand](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/28642676/)
- [International Society of Sports Nutrition, Creatine position stand](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC5469049/)

## Related resources

- [High-protein meal ideas](/resources/protein)


### How to Do a Chin-Up: A Practical Progression From Your First Rep to More Reps

Source: https://marinlazic.com/insights/how-to-do-a-chin-up
Published: 2026-02-28. Revised: 2026-10-14.

Most adults can get their first chin up in 8 to 12 weeks with three short sessions a week. The route is dead hangs, then rows, then negatives, then the first rep.

A chin-up uses an underhand grip with palms facing you. It trains the lats, biceps, forearms and trunk. The timeline varies with body mass, training history, grip strength, shoulder comfort and practice. Treat this plan as a starting point, not a promise.

## How do you set up for a chin up?

Use a secure bar that can support your body weight. Stand on a box if you need help reaching it. Take a supinated grip around shoulder width, or a little narrower if that feels better on your wrists. Wrap your thumbs around the bar.

Start with your arms straight and your body still. Keep your ribs down, gently brace your abdomen and keep your legs quiet. Pull your elbows towards your sides. Rise until your chin is over the bar without craning your neck. Lower with control until your elbows are straight, if that range feels comfortable.

A full range is a useful goal, but do not force a painful position. A shorter range can be a sensible temporary option while you build control. Avoid swinging, kicking and rushing the lowering phase. These can change the exercise and make it harder to judge progress.

## What is the progression to your first chin up?

### 1. Build tolerance and pulling strength

Start with two or three sessions each week. Leave at least a day between hard pulling sessions. Choose a level that lets you keep a steady body position.

- **Dead hangs:** Begin with 10 to 20 seconds for two or three sets. Stop before grip failure or shoulder pain.
- **Inverted rows:** Pull your chest towards a secure bar. Raise the bar or bend your knees to make them easier. Try two or three sets of 6 to 12 controlled repetitions.
- **Scapular movement:** From a supported hang, gently draw the shoulder blades down while keeping the elbows straight. Use two or three sets of 5 to 10 repetitions.

These are options, not tests. If a hang irritates your shoulder, use a supported version with your feet on a box or choose rows until you can tolerate hanging.

### 2. Practise the lowering phase

Step or climb to the top position. Keep your chin over the bar, then lower smoothly. Start with two or three sets of two to five repetitions. A lowering phase of about three to five seconds is a useful practice target, but it does not need to be exact.

Use enough rest to repeat the movement without dropping. If you cannot control the descent, use a higher box, a band or a lighter assistance setting. The goal is repeatable practice, not exhaustion.

### 3. Use assistance for full repetitions

A resistance band, assisted machine or foot on a box can reduce the load. Choose the option that lets you use the same controlled path.

Do two or three sets of 4 to 8 repetitions. Reduce assistance gradually, without swinging or losing shoulder control. Record the method because band strength and machine settings are not directly comparable.

### 4. Test an unassisted rep

After your warm-up, try one unassisted repetition while fresh. Keep the attempt clean. If you miss, return to assisted work rather than repeating maximal attempts until your grip or shoulders are tired.

Once you have one controlled rep, use small sets. For example, you might perform several sets of one repetition, then add a repetition to one set when that feels manageable. Rest as needed. The example is **illustrative, not a real client result or a guaranteed programme**.

## How do you get from one chin up to more?

Progressive resistance training is the basis for getting stronger. The American College of Sports Medicine position stand recommends that programme choices reflect your goal, physical capacity and training status, rather than a single compulsory set, rep or frequency rule. [Read the ACSM position stand](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/19204579/).

For chin-ups, progress one variable at a time. You could use less band assistance, add one controlled repetition, add a set, or improve your range. Keep one or two repetitions in reserve when technique starts to deteriorate. When you can perform several sets of controlled repetitions, a small amount of added load may be appropriate. Build it gradually and keep the same standards for the start, finish and lowering phase.

Record your grip, assistance, repetitions and any symptoms. Compare your own sessions rather than treating a device score or a single workout as a diagnosis of readiness.

## What if chin ups hurt your elbows or shoulders?

Muscle effort and mild next-day soreness can occur. Sharp pain, increasing joint pain, numbness, unusual weakness or a feeling of instability is a reason to stop and seek assessment from a qualified health professional. Stop exercise and seek prompt medical help for chest pain, unusual shortness of breath or light-headedness. [Harvard Health lists these as warning signs that should not be pushed through](https://www.health.harvard.edu/pain/safe-exercise-know-the-warning-signs-of-pushing-too-hard).

If you have a recent shoulder, elbow, wrist or neck injury, a diagnosed condition, or medicines that affect exercise tolerance, ask your doctor or physiotherapist how to modify the movement. This article is general education, not an individual diagnosis or treatment plan.

For related training context, read the [performance insights](/insights). If you want individual programming, use [apply for coaching](/apply). You can also [take the Performance Assessment](/assessment) for a broader review of strength and performance measures.

## Sources

- [American College of Sports Medicine position stand: Progression models in resistance training for healthy adults](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/19204579/)
- [Harvard Health Publishing: Safe exercise and warning signs](https://www.health.harvard.edu/pain/safe-exercise-know-the-warning-signs-of-pushing-too-hard)

## Related resources

- [Low-effort movement practice](/resources/groove)


### VO2 Max for Executives: A Useful Fitness and Longevity Metric

Source: https://marinlazic.com/insights/vo2-max-for-executives-longevity-metric
Published: 2025-11-15. Revised: 2026-10-14.

VO2 max is the strongest single fitness predictor of how long you live. Two to three easy aerobic sessions a week plus one hard one will raise it at any age.

## Key takeaways

VO2 max, or maximal oxygen uptake, measures how much oxygen your body can use during hard exercise. It is reported in millilitres of oxygen per kilogram of body weight per minute (ml/kg/min).

Higher cardiorespiratory fitness is associated with lower long-term mortality. A large retrospective study of 122,007 adults referred for treadmill testing found a graded association between fitness and survival. The study does not prove that raising VO2 max will extend an individual’s life, and its patients may not represent every executive or healthy adult. [Read the JAMA Network Open study](https://jamanetwork.com/journals/jamanetworkopen/fullarticle/2707428).

VO2 max is useful data, not a verdict on your health, leadership or lifespan. There is no universal minimum score that guarantees longevity. Age, sex, training history, body size, health conditions and the test method all affect the result.

## What does VO2 max measure?

During exercise, your lungs take in oxygen, your heart and blood vessels deliver it, and your muscles use it to produce energy. VO2 max reflects the combined capacity of that system. It is one part of fitness. It does not directly diagnose stress, cognitive performance, burnout or disease.

A higher result can make everyday aerobic work feel easier, but it does not guarantee better concentration, stress tolerance or work output. Sleep, nutrition, strength, workload and mental health also matter. For related strength work, see [how to do a chin-up](/insights/how-to-do-a-chin-up).

## What is a good VO2 max for your age?

Laboratory testing with a graded exercise test and metabolic cart gives a direct measurement. A watch or other wearable usually provides an estimate based on heart rate, pace, power and personal data. These estimates can be useful for trends, but their absolute accuracy varies.

Age-based tables can offer broad context, but they are not a personal prescription. Compare results from the same method, under similar conditions, and allow for normal day-to-day variation. A small change may reflect hydration, illness, heat, fatigue or device error.

A field test such as a timed walk or run can be practical for some people. It is still an estimate and may be unsuitable if you have symptoms, an injury or limited exercise experience. A qualified clinician or exercise professional can help choose a test.

## How do you improve VO2 max around a busy schedule?

There is no single session plan that suits every executive. Start with a workload you can repeat and progress gradually. The American Heart Association recommends at least 150 minutes of moderate aerobic activity per week, or 75 minutes of vigorous activity, plus muscle-strengthening work on at least two days. Build towards that level if you are currently inactive. [See the AHA adult activity recommendations](https://www.heart.org/en/healthy-living/fitness/fitness-basics/aha-recs-for-physical-activity-in-adults).

A simple structure is:

1. **Easy aerobic work.** Use brisk walking, cycling, rowing, swimming or another low-impact option. You should be able to speak in short sentences. Begin with two sessions of 20 to 40 minutes and add time slowly.
2. **Strength training.** Train major movement patterns two or more days each week. Strength supports daily function and helps you tolerate aerobic training, but it is not a prerequisite for a particular VO2 max score.
3. **Harder intervals.** After several consistent weeks, consider one interval session each week. For example, complete four short efforts at a hard but controlled pace, with easy recovery between them. The duration and intensity should match your experience and health status. More intensity is not always better.
4. **Recovery.** Keep easy days between demanding sessions. Check how you are sleeping, moving and feeling. Do not force a hard session when you are unwell or unusually fatigued.

**Illustrative session example, not a real client result:** 10 minutes easy, four repetitions of 3 minutes at a hard controlled effort with 3 minutes easy between them, then 5 to 10 minutes easy. This is a template, not a guarantee of improvement. A coach or clinician should adapt it to your history and goals.

Track attendance, duration, perceived effort and, where useful, a consistent test result. HRV and resting heart rate are best treated as within-person, device-specific trends. They do not provide a certain diagnosis of readiness or recovery. A cold plunge cannot guarantee a better HRV, VO2 max or work performance. For context on using HRV data, see [this HRV guide](/insights/how-to-boost-your-hrv).

## Is VO2 max training safe for executives over 40?

Speak with a healthcare professional before vigorous training if you have known heart, lung or metabolic disease, take medicines that affect exercise response, have been inactive for a long period, or are unsure whether hard exercise is appropriate. Stop and seek prompt medical care for chest pain, fainting, severe breathlessness or new concerning symptoms.

## What should you do first?

VO2 max is a valuable measure of cardiorespiratory fitness and a sensible trend to monitor when the testing method is consistent. It is associated with long-term health outcomes, but it cannot predict an individual’s lifespan or replace clinical care.

Start with regular aerobic movement, add strength work, introduce intensity gradually and protect recovery. If you want help interpreting your data and building a plan, [take the Performance Assessment](/assessment) or [apply for coaching](/apply). Any plan should be based on your history, current capacity, schedule and goals.

## Sources

- [Mandsager et al., Association of Cardiorespiratory Fitness and Mortality Among Adults Undergoing Exercise Treadmill Testing, JAMA Network Open](https://jamanetwork.com/journals/jamanetworkopen/fullarticle/2707428)
- [American Heart Association Recommendations for Physical Activity in Adults](https://www.heart.org/en/healthy-living/fitness/fitness-basics/aha-recs-for-physical-activity-in-adults)

## Related resources

- [4-week base-building example](/resources/engine)
- [Training for long-term health](/training-for-long-term-health)


### A Founder’s Guide to a Practical Stress Management System

Source: https://marinlazic.com/insights/founder-guide-stress-management-system
Published: 2025-11-28. Revised: 2026-10-14.

Founders do not need a mindset. They need a review process: workload, sleep, training and recovery looked at together every week.

Stress is a normal response to challenge. It becomes a concern when it stays high, feels overwhelming, or starts to affect sleep, mood, work or relationships. A useful system makes those signals easier to notice and gives you a few low-risk actions to try.

This guide is educational. It is not a diagnosis or a substitute for medical or mental health care.

## Which stress signals should a founder track?

Allostatic load describes the cumulative cost of adapting to repeated stress. It is a research concept, not a result that can be diagnosed from one wearable reading. Work demands, sleep, illness, training, alcohol, travel and personal circumstances can all affect how you feel and perform.

Heart rate variability (HRV) is the variation in time between heartbeats. It can provide context about autonomic regulation, but it is not a standalone stress biomarker. There is no agreed normal HRV range. A reading is most useful as a trend against your own baseline, collected with the same device and similar conditions. Wearable measurements can differ from ECG measurements, especially during movement or mental stress. [Research review on HRV applications in strength and conditioning](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC11204851/)

Use HRV as one input alongside sleep, resting heart rate, training load, mood and your own symptoms. A low reading does not prove that you are unwell, and a high reading does not prove that you are ready for hard work. Avoid using arbitrary cut-offs such as “below 40” or “above 70” as universal labels.

## What does a daily stress management system look like?

### Morning check-in

Take two minutes to record:

1. Sleep duration and how rested you feel.
2. Mood, energy and physical symptoms.
3. Planned training and the main demands of the day.
4. Optional HRV or resting heart rate, measured consistently.

If several signals look worse than usual, reduce optional intensity. Keep essential work, eat regularly, take a short walk and plan an earlier night. One difficult morning is information, not a verdict.

### Micro-resets during work

Choose one practice for one to five minutes:

- Breathe slowly and comfortably, with a slightly longer exhale. Stop if you feel dizzy, panicky or short of breath.
- Walk away from the screen and look into the distance.
- Relax your jaw and shoulders, then name the next small task.
- Use a brief mindfulness or progressive muscle relaxation practice.

In a randomised 28-day trial, brief breathing practices were linked with better daily mood and lower state anxiety. The study also reported improvements in respiratory measures. It did not find significant changes in HRV, resting heart rate or sleep, so do not promise a sleep or recovery result from a breathing drill. [Cell Reports Medicine trial](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC9873947/)

### Evening recovery

Keep the last part of the day quieter where possible. Dim lights, reduce stimulating work, prepare for tomorrow and use a reading, relaxation or journalling routine that suits you. A consistent sleep schedule and enough time in bed matter more than a perfect ritual. If sleep problems continue, discuss them with a GP.

### Movement and training

Regular aerobic and resistance exercise can support physical and mental health. Start at a level you can repeat. Brisk walking, cycling, strength training and outdoor time are reasonable options. Zone 2 is a coaching label, not a universal prescription. You do not need to chase a particular heart-rate percentage to benefit from steady movement.

## When is it burnout, and when should you see a professional?

The World Health Organization classifies burnout as an occupational phenomenon, not a medical condition. It relates specifically to chronic workplace stress that has not been successfully managed and includes exhaustion, mental distance or cynicism about work, and reduced professional efficacy. [WHO definition of burnout](https://www.who.int/news/item/28-05-2019-burn-out-an-occupational-phenomenon-international-classification-of-diseases)

Coaching habits may help with planning and behaviour. They cannot diagnose depression, anxiety, trauma, sleep disorders or other medical conditions. Speak with a GP or mental health professional if distress persists, functioning declines, sleep or appetite changes significantly, or you rely on alcohol or other substances to cope. Seek urgent help for thoughts of self-harm. In Australia, call 000 in an emergency, or contact [healthdirect](https://www.healthdirect.gov.au/stress) for health advice and referral options.

## How do you run a weekly stress review?

The following is an **illustrative template, not a real client result**:

- Record sleep, mood, symptoms and optional HRV on most mornings.
- Choose two repeatable movement sessions and one short breathing practice.
- Review the week for patterns, without treating any number as a diagnosis.
- Keep what helps. Remove what adds pressure. Raise persistent concerns with a clinician.

For more detail, read [How to Boost Your HRV](/insights/how-to-boost-your-hrv) and [How to Improve Sleep Quality](/insights/how-to-improve-sleep-quality). For individual context, you can use the [Performance Assessment](/assessment). You can also explore the [insights library](/insights).

## Sources

- [World Health Organization: burnout as an occupational phenomenon](https://www.who.int/news/item/28-05-2019-burn-out-an-occupational-phenomenon-international-classification-of-diseases)
- [Balban et al., Cell Reports Medicine: brief structured respiration practices](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC9873947/)
- [Addleman et al., HRV applications in strength and conditioning](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC11204851/)
- [healthdirect: stress and when to seek help](https://www.healthdirect.gov.au/stress)

## Related resources

- [Daily recovery checklist](/resources/recover)


### Zone 2 Training for Busy Professionals: A Practical Guide

Source: https://marinlazic.com/insights/zone-2-training-busy-professionals
Published: 2025-12-10. Revised: 2026-10-14.

Zone 2 is the pace where you can still speak in full sentences. Two 45 minute sessions a week is enough for most busy professionals to build an aerobic base.

## Key takeaways

Zone 2 is a useful name for steady, low-intensity aerobic exercise below the first lactate threshold. It can support cardiorespiratory fitness and provide an easier way to add regular movement. It is not proven to be the single best intensity for every goal. A 2025 review found that current evidence does not support Zone 2 as the optimal intensity for mitochondrial or fat-oxidation outcomes, especially when total training time is low. [Read the review on PubMed](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/40560504/)

Use Zone 2 as one part of a training week. Adults should aim for at least 150 minutes of moderate activity across the week, plus muscle-strengthening work on two or more days, according to the [World Health Organization](https://www.who.int/initiatives/behealthy/physical-activity). Any amount is better than none. Your best starting dose is one you can repeat without worsening pain, illness or excessive fatigue.

## What should Zone 2 feel like?

The label varies between heart-rate systems. Fixed percentages of maximum heart rate can misclassify intensity because people differ in fitness, medication, heat response and measurement accuracy. A practical cue is the talk test. At moderate intensity, you can talk but not sing, as explained by the [US Centers for Disease Control and Prevention](https://www.cdc.gov/physical-activity-basics/measuring/index.html). For an easier aerobic session, keep the effort comfortable and controlled. If speech becomes broken, reduce resistance or pace.

A laboratory test can estimate thresholds more precisely, but it is not necessary for most people. Wrist heart-rate data can help you notice patterns. Treat it as an estimate, not a medical measurement. Choose a bike, brisk walk, rower, incline treadmill or similar activity. The best mode is the one that fits your schedule and does not aggravate an injury.

## How many Zone 2 sessions a week do you need?

Start with two sessions of 30 to 45 minutes, including an easy warm-up and cool-down. After two or three weeks, add time only if recovery is good. A longer session is optional. It is not a requirement for progress.

This **illustrative template is not a real client result**:

- Monday: full-body strength training.
- Tuesday: 35 to 45 minutes of easy aerobic work at a conversational effort.
- Wednesday: rest or an easy walk.
- Thursday: full-body strength training.
- Friday or Saturday: 40 to 60 minutes of steady aerobic work.
- One optional higher-intensity session, only when sleep, health and recovery are stable.
- At least one complete rest day.

You can split a session into shorter blocks when work is busy. Consistency matters more than a perfect schedule. Keep strength training in the week because aerobic work does not replace muscle-strengthening exercise.

## What adaptations can you expect?

Training can improve how efficiently you perform a given workload, but the size and timing of change vary. Do not promise a fixed fall in resting heart rate, a fixed rise in HRV, better sleep within a set number of weeks or a guaranteed change in body composition. Track a few simple measures instead: duration, pace or power at a similar effort, perceived exertion, and how you feel later that day and the next morning.

HRV is affected by sleep, stress, alcohol, illness, breathing, posture and the device itself. Compare your own readings from the same device and similar conditions over time. A single score is not a diagnosis and does not prove readiness or poor recovery. A lower reading is a prompt to consider the wider picture, not a reason to panic or cancel every session. For related practical guidance, see [how to boost your HRV](/insights/how-to-boost-your-hrv).

Breathing practice may help mood for some people, but it is not a substitute for treatment or a guaranteed sleep intervention. In one randomised trial, a month of brief breathwork improved daily mood measures and reduced respiratory rate, while the researchers found no significant changes in HRV, resting heart rate or sleep measures. [Read the trial on PMC](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC9873947/)

## When should you skip a Zone 2 session?

Stop exercise and seek medical advice for chest pain, fainting, unexplained severe breathlessness, new palpitations or other alarming symptoms. Get individual advice before changing training if you have cardiovascular, respiratory, metabolic or kidney disease, are pregnant, take medicines that affect heart rate, or are returning after a significant illness or injury. A coach can help with programming, but cannot diagnose or prescribe treatment.

## What should you do first?

Begin with two repeatable sessions, use the talk test, and record how training fits with sleep and work. Adjust the plan when symptoms or recovery change. For individual programming, you can [apply for coaching](/apply) or [book a Performance Assessment](/assessment). These services do not replace medical care.

## Sources

- [Storoschuk et al., “Much Ado About Zone 2”, PubMed](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/40560504/)
- [World Health Organization, Physical activity guidance](https://www.who.int/initiatives/behealthy/physical-activity)
- [CDC, How to measure physical activity intensity](https://www.cdc.gov/physical-activity-basics/measuring/index.html)
- [Balban et al., breathwork randomised trial, PMC](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC9873947/)

## Related resources

- [4-week base-building example](/resources/engine)


### Morning Routines for Executives: Use Data, Not Podcasts

Source: https://marinlazic.com/insights/morning-routine-executives-data-not-podcasts
Published: 2025-12-22. Revised: 2026-10-14.

The best morning routine for an executive is a regular wake time, 10 minutes of outdoor light and a look at last night's sleep data. Nothing else is required.

Waking at 5 am is not a requirement for success. A useful morning routine starts with enough sleep, a consistent schedule where possible, and a first hour that supports the work you need to do. Your wake time should fit your sleep needs, commitments and natural preference. Adults aged 18 to 60 are generally advised to get at least seven hours of sleep regularly, although individual needs vary. [American Academy of Sleep Medicine and Sleep Research Society](https://aasm.org/aasm-and-srs-publish-new-sleep-duration-consensus-statement/)

## Why does the morning routine start the night before?

An early alarm cannot make up for a late bedtime. If you need to wake earlier, move bedtime gradually and protect the total time available for sleep. A 5 am start that leaves you tired is a poor trade.

Notice when you naturally become sleepy, when you feel alert, and what your workday requires. Use those observations to set a realistic wake time. If you snore loudly, gasp during sleep, wake with headaches, or feel very sleepy during the day, speak with a GP or sleep clinician. A routine cannot diagnose or treat a sleep disorder.

## What does the cortisol awakening response tell you?

The cortisol awakening response, or CAR, is the rise in cortisol seen during the first 30 to 45 minutes after waking. Reviews describe it as part of the body’s preparation for the active part of the day. Its size varies with sleep, stress, timing, light and other factors. It is not a simple personal score for resilience, productivity or health. [Endocrine Reviews](https://www.endocrine.org/journals/endocrine-reviews/the-cortisol-awakening-response)

You do not need to measure cortisol to build a useful morning. Avoid presenting a difficult morning as proof that your CAR is “dysregulated”. Persistent fatigue, low mood, anxiety, or major changes in sleep deserve a clinical assessment rather than a supplement or tracking plan.

## How much morning light do you need?

Light is a major timing cue for the body clock. Daylight helps synchronise the circadian system, while bright light at night can affect sleep timing. Research reviews support daylight as a useful part of a regular sleep-wake pattern, but the response depends on intensity, timing and the person. [Review of light, circadian rhythms, sleep and mood](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC6751071/)

Try going outside soon after waking when practical. Stay out long enough to get useful daylight, and repeat the habit across the week. Do not stare at the sun. On dark mornings, indoors, or in unsafe weather, use ordinary safe lighting and ask a clinician before using a bright-light device, especially if you have an eye condition or a history of mood episodes.

Light is a cue, not a guarantee. Judge the habit by your sleep and daytime function over several weeks.

## What does a 60 minute executive morning routine look like?

This is an **illustrative template, not a real client result or a prescription**. Adjust it to your schedule, health needs and preferences.

- **First 5 minutes:** Get up, drink water if thirsty, and avoid rushing straight into messages.
- **Next 10 to 20 minutes:** Get outdoor daylight when safe and practical.
- **Next 10 to 20 minutes:** Walk, stretch, or do easy mobility. Save hard training for a time that suits your programme and recovery.
- **Next 10 minutes:** Review the day. Choose one important task and identify the first small step.
- **Remaining time:** Eat if hungry, prepare for work, or begin a focused block without opening every communication channel at once.

Breakfast is optional. Some people prefer food soon after waking. Others do not. A protein-containing meal can be useful for people who enjoy it or train in the morning, but skipping breakfast is not automatically harmful and a protein-rich breakfast is not essential for everyone. Caffeine timing and amount should reflect your sensitivity, sleep and medical context. If caffeine worsens anxiety, palpitations or sleep, discuss it with a health professional.

## How should you track whether the routine works?

HRV from a wearable can help you observe within-person trends. Readings are device-specific and affected by sleep, alcohol, illness, training, stress and measurement conditions. A single low value does not diagnose a problem or prove that you are unready to work or train. Use the same device and similar conditions, then compare the trend with how you feel and perform. HRV is not a substitute for medical assessment.

A simple weekly note can include bedtime, wake time, daylight, caffeine, training, mood and energy. Change one variable at a time when possible.

Do not use cold exposure as a promise of better focus, recovery or health. It may feel stimulating, yet individual responses and risks vary. People with cardiovascular disease, fainting, pregnancy, or other relevant conditions should seek medical advice before using deliberate cold exposure.

## How do you keep a morning routine going?

Start with two actions: protect a realistic sleep window and get daylight when practical. Add movement or planning only if it helps. Review the routine after two to four weeks using sleep, energy, concentration and work quality rather than a social-media standard.

For a broader review of sleep habits, read [how to improve sleep quality](/insights/how-to-improve-sleep-quality). For an individual performance discussion, visit the [assessment](/assessment) page or read about how to [apply for coaching](/apply). Coaching does not replace medical care, diagnosis or treatment.

## Sources

- [American Academy of Sleep Medicine and Sleep Research Society: adult sleep duration consensus](https://aasm.org/aasm-and-srs-publish-new-sleep-duration-consensus-statement/)
- [Blume, Garbazza and Spitschan: Effects of light on human circadian rhythms, sleep and mood](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC6751071/)
- [Stalder and colleagues: The Cortisol Awakening Response](https://www.endocrine.org/journals/endocrine-reviews/the-cortisol-awakening-response)

## Related resources

- [Daily movement routine](/resources/routine)


### Executive Fitness After 40: A Practical Strength, Cardio and Recovery Plan

Source: https://marinlazic.com/insights/executive-fitness-program-strength-cardio-recovery
Published: 2026-01-05. Revised: 2026-10-14.

After 40, the priority order is strength twice a week, easy cardio three times a week, and sleep protected above both. Supplements come last.

Strength, aerobic fitness and recovery remain trainable after 40. Regular resistance training supports strength and function, while aerobic work supports cardiorespiratory fitness. Sleep, food and workload shape recovery.

This guide is a coaching framework, not a diagnosis or a promise of a particular result. A GP should review unexplained fatigue, chest pain, fainting, persistent pain, major sleep problems or symptoms that affect daily life. Get medical clearance before hard training if you have a relevant condition or take medicines that may affect exercise or supplements.

## What changes with age?

Muscle strength, power and bone density can change across adulthood, particularly when activity falls. The practical response is to train the capacities you want to keep: resistance exercise for major movement patterns, regular aerobic work and frequent walking. Build a routine that survives travel and busy periods.

## What does a weekly training plan look like after 40?

The following is an **illustrative session template, not a real client result or a guaranteed prescription**. Adjust it to your training history, technique, schedule and health status.

- **Day 1, full-body strength:** squat or leg press, bench press or push-up, row, hip hinge and a loaded carry or plank. Use controlled sets with a load that leaves a few good repetitions in reserve.
- **Day 2, aerobic work:** 25 to 45 minutes at a conversational pace, such as brisk walking, cycling or rowing. Add short harder intervals only if you already tolerate them and have no relevant medical concerns.
- **Day 3, full-body strength:** split squat or step-up, overhead press, pulldown or chin-up progression, Romanian deadlift and an anti-rotation core exercise.
- **Other days:** easy walking, mobility work or complete rest. Keep at least one easier day between demanding strength sessions when possible.

Begin with two strength sessions if three are unrealistic. Two consistent sessions are more useful than an ambitious plan that gets skipped. See our guide on [how to do a chin up](/insights/how-to-do-a-chin-up).

Choose a weight you can lift with steady technique. A useful starting point is two to four sets of roughly 5 to 12 repetitions for most exercises. Power work needs extra care: use simple, low-risk movements such as fast but controlled medicine-ball throws or step-ups, and stop before technique deteriorates. A coach can help select safer variations.

## How do you progress without chasing numbers?

Track exercises, sets, repetitions, effort and symptoms. When repetitions feel controlled, add a small amount of weight, one repetition, or a set. Change one variable at a time. If sleep, work stress or joint symptoms worsen, reduce volume or intensity.

Progressive overload means gradually asking the body to do more over time. It does not require maximal lifts. Good technique, repeatable sessions and appropriate recovery matter more than testing a one-repetition maximum every week.

## How much cardio do you need after 40?

Cardio trains the heart, lungs and working muscles. Choose activities you can repeat. A mix of easy aerobic work and occasional harder efforts can be useful, but the dose depends on fitness and medical context. VO2 max is informative, yet an association with health outcomes does not guarantee a particular lifespan or outcome.

Protect a regular sleep opportunity. A common target is 7 to 9 hours, but sleep need varies. Keep wake time consistent, limit late caffeine and alcohol, and seek assessment for loud snoring, breathing pauses or persistent daytime sleepiness.

Slow breathing may help you pause during a demanding day. In a randomised trial of five-minute daily practice, mood measures improved, but HRV, resting heart rate and sleep did not change significantly. [Read the trial report](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC9873947/).

Treat wearable HRV as a personal trend. Sleep, alcohol, illness, training, stress and hydration can all affect it. Do not use one score to establish readiness or diagnose a problem. [Wearable HRV measurement has limits](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC10742885/).

## What should an executive over 40 eat, and is creatine worth it?

Eat enough food to support training. Include protein-rich foods, vegetables, fruit, wholegrains and fluids. Protein targets should reflect body size, training, diet and medical needs. A dietitian can help with kidney disease, gastrointestinal illness or weight-management concerns.

Creatine is optional. The most studied form is **creatine monohydrate**. For a healthy adult who chooses to use it, a common maintenance approach is 3 to 5 g per day, with individual suitability considered. A loading phase is not mandatory, and there is no universal requirement to use 0.1 g/kg per day. The [International Society of Sports Nutrition position stand](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC5469049/) and [NIH Office of Dietary Supplements guidance](https://ods.od.nih.gov/factsheets/ExerciseAndAthleticPerformance-HealthProfessional/) describe its strongest evidence in repeated, high-intensity exercise and note that responses vary.

Choose a product with transparent ingredients and independent, third-party batch testing where available. Evidence for cognitive benefits remains uncertain. If you have kidney disease, abnormal kidney tests, are pregnant, or take medicines that may affect kidney function, discuss creatine with a clinician. Creatinine blood results may change with creatine use without proving kidney injury.

## When should you see a doctor before training?

A qualified strength coach can adapt exercise selection and progression. A GP, physiotherapist, sports physician, sleep clinician, psychologist or dietitian should be involved when symptoms, injury, medication, sleep breathing or medical conditions fall outside coaching scope. Seek urgent care for chest pressure, severe breathlessness, fainting or sudden neurological symptoms.

For a tailored starting point, use the [Performance Assessment](/assessment) or [apply](/apply) page. Any plan should begin with your history, current capacity, goals and constraints.

## Sources

- [International Society of Sports Nutrition position stand on creatine](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC5469049/)
- [NIH Office of Dietary Supplements: Dietary Supplements for Exercise and Athletic Performance](https://ods.od.nih.gov/factsheets/ExerciseAndAthleticPerformance-HealthProfessional/)
- [Randomised trial of brief structured respiration practices](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC9873947/)
- [Review of wearable heart-rate variability measurement](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC10742885/)

### CEO Burnout Recovery Protocol: A Practical, Evidence-Aware Starting Point

Source: https://marinlazic.com/insights/ceo-burnout-recovery-protocol
Published: 2026-01-18. Revised: 2026-10-14.

Burnout is a workload problem before it is a fitness problem. Cut the load first, then rebuild sleep, then training.

## What is burnout?

Burnout is not simply low fitness or a lack of discipline. The [World Health Organization describes burnout](https://www.who.int/standards/classifications/frequently-asked-questions/burn-out-an-occupational-phenomenon) as an occupational phenomenon linked to chronic workplace stress that has not been managed successfully. It involves exhaustion, greater mental distance or cynicism about work, and reduced professional efficacy. It is not classified as a medical condition in ICD-11.

That distinction matters. A coach can help with routines, training, workload habits and recovery. A coach cannot diagnose depression, anxiety, sleep disorders, cardiovascular disease or other causes of fatigue. If symptoms are persistent, severe or worsening, speak with a GP or qualified mental health professional. Seek urgent help for thoughts of self-harm, chest pain, fainting or severe breathlessness.

## What is the order of recovery from burnout?

Recovery starts with reducing the load that is driving the problem. Review the next two weeks of work and remove, delegate or postpone tasks that are not essential. Set a clear end to the workday where possible. Protect time for meals, movement and sleep. Lower demand is often more useful than another demanding protocol.

Next, establish a simple baseline. Record sleep duration, energy, training, alcohol intake and key work stressors for several weeks. A wearable can add context, though it does not replace symptoms or clinical assessment.

Build training around recovery capacity. Two or three moderate resistance sessions each week may be appropriate for some people. Easy aerobic work, walking and light mobility can support regular movement without creating another performance test. Keep hard intervals and maximal lifting limited while sleep and energy are unstable. Progress gradually when daily function, mood and sleep are improving.

An illustrative session example, not a real client result, might be a 30-minute easy cycle followed by two moderate sets each of a squat pattern, press and row. Stop or reduce the session for pain, dizziness or unusual breathlessness.

## How do sleep and breathing help burnout recovery?

Keep a consistent wake time and reduce late caffeine, alcohol and bright screens when they interfere with sleep. The existing guide on [how to improve sleep quality](/insights/how-to-improve-sleep-quality) can help with the routine side of this work. Snoring, gasping, witnessed pauses in breathing, persistent insomnia or marked daytime sleepiness warrant a GP discussion rather than a self-directed sleep challenge.

Brief breathing practice may be a low-risk way to create a pause during a demanding day. In a randomised study, 5 minutes a day of structured breathing over one month improved mood measures and reduced respiratory rate. The study found no significant change in HRV, resting heart rate or sleep measures, so it does not support claims of a guaranteed sleep or recovery result. Read the [full trial](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC9873947/) for its methods and limits. Avoid forceful breath holding or rapid breathing if it causes dizziness, panic or other symptoms.

## Can HRV tell you if you are burnt out?

Heart rate variability is the variation in time between heartbeats. Treat it as a personal trend, not a score for health, burnout or readiness. Measurements vary with the device, position, time of day, illness, alcohol, sleep and breathing pattern. Compare readings under similar conditions and look for a sustained change alongside sleep, mood, resting heart rate and training response.

A low reading on one morning does not prove that you are overtrained. A higher reading does not prove that you are recovered. Ask whether the trend agrees with how you feel and function. If the signals disagree, choose the safer training option and seek medical advice when symptoms persist. The guide on [how to boost HRV](/insights/how-to-boost-your-hrv) is best read as a routine guide, not a diagnostic tool. Cold-water exposure may feel refreshing for some people, but it has no guarantee of improving HRV, burnout or long-term health.

## When is coaching the right step, and when is it a doctor?

Coaching can help you turn a medical or psychological care plan into practical habits. It can also help you review training load, schedule recovery, prepare questions for a clinician and monitor routine changes. It should not replace diagnosis, therapy, medication management or treatment for sleep and breathing disorders.

A useful first step is a [Performance Assessment](/assessment). Bring your goals, training, sleep pattern, work demands and medical advice. The aim is a plan that fits your actual capacity, with progress judged by function and wellbeing rather than a single wearable score.

## Sources

- [World Health Organization: Burn-out an occupational phenomenon](https://www.who.int/standards/classifications/frequently-asked-questions/burn-out-an-occupational-phenomenon)
- [Balban et al., 2023: Brief structured respiration practices enhance mood](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC9873947/)

- [Daily recovery checklist](/resources/recover)


### Olympic Training Principles for Sustainable Business Performance

Source: https://marinlazic.com/insights/olympic-training-principles-business-performance
Published: 2026-01-30. Revised: 2026-10-14.

Olympic athletes train in blocks with planned easy weeks. Executives who copy that structure recover better and perform more consistently than those who push every week.

## Key takeaways

- Elite sport offers useful planning ideas for demanding work, but business is not an Olympic event. Adapt the principles rather than copying an athlete’s programme.
- Plan periods of focused work, lighter work and review. Protect sleep, movement, food and time away from work.
- Use training load, mood, sleep and heart-rate data as prompts for reflection. They are not proof of readiness, illness or performance.
- Burnout is an occupational phenomenon linked to chronic workplace stress. Persistent or severe symptoms need qualified health support.

## What can business learn from Olympic training?

Athletes work towards a clear event, with a defined plan and planned recovery. Leaders and teams also face periods of high demand. The useful parallel is the planning process, not a claim that business and sport have the same risks or goals.

A practical performance plan names the outcome, preparation work, work to reduce or delegate, and the point for recovery and review. This makes trade-offs visible to a team.

## How do you periodise a business year?

In sport, periodisation means organising training stress and recovery over time. A business version can be simple and flexible:

- **Preparation:** clarify priorities, set decision rules, build skills and remove avoidable work.
- **Focus:** give a small number of important projects protected attention. Keep meetings and new commitments under control.
- **Deload and review:** reduce non-essential work after a demanding push. Review what worked, repair relationships and update the plan.
- **Renewal:** take proper time away from work. Return with a short list of priorities rather than a full backlog.

These phases are an **illustrative template, not a real client result or a universal prescription**. Organisations have different constraints, so do not force a fixed annual cycle onto continuous service.

A weekly version may be more useful. Choose one or two priority outcomes, schedule demanding tasks when concentration is usually strongest, and place lighter administration around them. Set a stop time where possible. Treat recovery as part of the plan, not as a reward for finishing everything.

## How do Olympic athletes manage load, and how can you?

Recovery includes sleep, regular meals, movement, social contact and time with no work demands. A short walk or quiet break may help, but no routine guarantees better performance. For practical sleep guidance, read [how to improve sleep quality](/insights/how-to-improve-sleep-quality).

Track the load of work as well as the hours. Useful questions include: How many high-stakes decisions did I make? How often was my attention interrupted? Did I have enough control and support? Have I had several nights of poor sleep?

The World Health Organization describes burnout as a syndrome resulting from chronic workplace stress that has not been successfully managed. It includes exhaustion, mental distance or cynicism about the job, and reduced professional efficacy. WHO classifies it as an occupational phenomenon, not a medical condition, and says it should not be used for every form of distress. [Read the WHO definition.](https://www.who.int/news/item/28-05-2019-burn-out-an-occupational-phenomenon-international-classification-of-diseases)

Coaching can help with habits, workload conversations and planning. It cannot diagnose depression, anxiety, sleep disorders, heart disease or other health conditions. Seek a GP or appropriately qualified mental health professional for persistent low mood, panic, severe exhaustion, major sleep problems, thoughts of self-harm, chest pain, fainting or unusual breathlessness. A workplace should address unreasonable demands and provide appropriate support.

## Which recovery tools transfer from sport to work?

Slow breathing or a brief breathing practice may be a reasonable way to pause and settle. In a randomised study of daily breathing exercises, mood and some breathing measures improved, while there were **no significant changes in HRV, resting heart rate or measured sleep outcomes** over the study period. [See the trial in *Cell Reports Medicine*.](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC9873947/)

Heart-rate variability (HRV) is the variation in time between heartbeats. Wearable readings depend on the device, measurement conditions and the person. Use the same device and similar conditions, and look at your own trend alongside sleep, illness, training and how you feel. A single score is not a diagnosis or a certain readiness decision. For more context, see [how to boost your HRV](/insights/how-to-boost-your-hrv). Do not use HRV to delay medical care.

Cold water exposure may feel refreshing for some people. It does not guarantee recovery, resilience or better business results. People with cardiovascular conditions, fainting history or other health concerns should ask a clinician before trying it.

## How do you review the week like a coach?

At the end of each week, record the key outcome, the work that created the most strain, and one recovery action. Review several weeks, then adjust commitments and keep margin for unexpected work.

A performance assessment can help organise these questions, but it is not a medical assessment. To discuss coaching scope and next steps, see [Apply for Coaching](/apply).

## Sources

- [World Health Organization: Burn-out as an occupational phenomenon](https://www.who.int/news/item/28-05-2019-burn-out-an-occupational-phenomenon-international-classification-of-diseases)
- [Cell Reports Medicine: Randomised breathing exercise trial](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC9873947/)
